![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/65491fb3de59e45bffb4774aca31cc25f20f555f18ffafc8d56221c689520380.png)

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1={\color{blue}-1},$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_2={\color{red}1},$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_3=0.$

Therefore, we get

In conclusion, we get $a=0,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-1.$

source.question: e-5505
source.value:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 6 & 0 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 6 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )([{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +2]-12) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(\lambda -5)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=4,$ $\lambda_2=5,$ and $\lambda_3=-2.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/2f943468de2124874c2d806db25c6ca91a2df9a74902af95220e4974e5ef483b.png)

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible  diagonal matrix is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/6f73d40195a91530d761d966db886e9ad2d87d7fc1059a4112a0a2701ce6a72f.png)

source.question: e-5506
source.value:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are  

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=-2, \quad$ $\lambda_2=-1, \quad$ $\lambda_3=2.$ 

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_1=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & 6 \\ -9 & -7 & 9 \\ -16 & -10 & 14\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 \\ -9 & -5 & 9 \\ -16 & -10 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 & 0 \\ -9 & -5 & 9 & 0 \\ -16 & -10 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{8}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{3} & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get $x_1=x_3.$
Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/fdf2311a1010ed8e8f25623328171687a63ea5da80f6e18a1a8dfbff9e5fae42.png)

Therefore, setting $x_3=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/34e8934a56885ec189cc1819b1336f5b52b7708a092233e3c20e0960218cad10.png)

Finally, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/ec378af1062dda61e89d060d565ef70bf7593a723bd3cba78dfd86f0d027dc5d.png)

source.question: e-7330
source.value:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=2,\quad$ $\lambda_2=1, \quad$ $\lambda_3=0.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For $\lambda_1=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives us the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/b88fd696293e4151a71ca12d25cb56821ba034e07a876777fa30d5d6f6b9c4c3.png)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives us the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/38941ad5615365437a1aee93f085b33d6a240c5a61ce8e0f0a10acb465de0f18.png)

- For $\lambda_3=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives us the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/a3ea884b0f6ba11582eb72e6cffcc871a144e55c446aaa304e1c7f9face13c7b.png)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069769/assets/cc87c4f07116bf301d115ffeb00e81f9cd25d21cb40f61fdbc310f86557a61b4.png)
